passage: In Gurpreet's village near Moga, people said you saw a doctor for fever and a granthi for worries. After her engagement broke off, she stopped sleeping and lost interest in the dairy work she loved. Her cousin Vandana, a nurse in the district hospital, visited on a Sunday. "There's a counsellor at the hospital on Thursdays," she said. Gurpreet laughed. "I'm not mad." Vandana shrugged. "You get your tractor serviced before it breaks. Same idea." Gurpreet thought about it all week. On Thursday she took the bus, a dupatta pulled over her face in case someone saw. The counsellor was a calm woman who mostly listened. Gurpreet went back three more times. She stopped hiding her face by the second visit.

qa.q: On which day was the counsellor at the hospital?
qa.a: The counsellor was there on Thursdays.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet pull her dupatta over her face on the bus?
qa.a: She was embarrassed and worried people would judge her for seeing a counsellor.

qa.q: What made Vandana's way of suggesting help effective?
qa.a: She compared counselling to routine tractor servicing, making it feel ordinary rather than a sign of being 'mad'.

qa.q: What would change if more people in the village saw counselling like Vandana does?
qa.a: People like Gurpreet might seek help sooner without hiding, because it would feel as normal as seeing a doctor.

grounding: Shows a young woman in a village coming to see counselling as ordinary care and choosing it despite stigma.

passage: Liam had been in Dublin eight months, working long hours at a design agency. He wasn't in crisis, just flat, snappy, and waking at four every morning. His flatmate Siddiq mentioned that he saw a therapist every other week. "For what?" Liam asked. "Nothing's wrong with you." Siddiq smiled. "That's sort of the point. I go so things don't get bad." Liam looked into his company's employee support scheme and found six free sessions. He wasn't sure whether he needed a therapist, a doctor or just more sleep, so he asked his GP first, who suggested talking therapy. The first session felt awkward. By the third, Liam noticed he was sleeping until six. He booked three more.

qa.q: How many free sessions did Liam's company scheme offer?
qa.a: It offered six free sessions.

qa.q: Why did Liam ask Siddiq 'For what?'
qa.a: He was surprised, because he believed therapy was only for people with something clearly wrong.

qa.q: What was sensible about how Liam chose his help?
qa.a: He wasn't sure what kind of support he needed, so he asked his GP first and then used the free sessions.

qa.q: How does Siddiq see therapy differently from Liam at first?
qa.a: Siddiq sees it as regular upkeep to stop problems growing, not as a last resort. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young man treating therapy as routine care and choosing suitable help through a doctor.

passage: The staff wellness room at the Jaipur software firm had a sign-up sheet for peer support circles on Wednesdays. Simran walked past it for a month. After a bad quarter and a breakup, she finally wrote her name down. Lalit from accounts ran the circle; he'd trained as a peer listener after his own rough year. "This isn't therapy," he said at the start. "It's people listening. If anyone needs more, I'll help you find a counsellor." Simran mostly listened the first week. In the second, she spoke about feeling like she was failing at everything. Afterward Lalit quietly gave her the card for the company's counselling service. She booked a session, relieved that it was both.

qa.q: On which day did the peer support circles meet?
qa.a: They met on Wednesdays.

qa.q: What might Simran walking past the sheet for a month suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was hesitant, perhaps unsure she needed help or worried what others would think.

qa.q: What made Lalit's circle a safe choice for Simran?
qa.a: He was clear about what the circle could and couldn't do, and pointed her to a counsellor when she needed more.

qa.q: How might Lalit see his role in the circle?
qa.a: He sees himself as a listener and a bridge to professional help, not a therapist, drawing on his own rough year.

grounding: Shows a young worker using peer support at work as ordinary care and being guided to counselling when needed.

passage:
Dear Asif,
You said on the phone that therapy is for people who are 'falling apart', so you'll manage. I used to think that too. I started seeing a counsellor last year, not because of a crisis, but because I kept snapping at my team and lying awake before Mondays. It's like going to the dentist before the tooth breaks. A few things I learnt about choosing: a counsellor or psychologist is for talking things through and learning skills; a psychiatrist is a doctor, for when things need a medical look; peer groups are for feeling less alone. I tried one counsellor who didn't fit and switched after two sessions, which is allowed. You mentioned your company has a free counselling line. Maybe just try one call? No pressure. Either way, I'm around this weekend if you want to go for a walk.
Love,
Irawati

qa.q: Why did Irawati start seeing a counsellor?
qa.a: Irawati kept snapping at the team and lying awake before Mondays; it was not because of a crisis.

qa.q: What does Asif's belief that therapy is for people 'falling apart' suggest about how Asif feels?
qa.a: Asif probably feels a need to manage alone and may be uneasy or ashamed about asking for help.

qa.q: What does Irawati suggest about choosing help?
qa.a: Know the difference between counsellors, psychiatrists and peer groups, switch if one does not fit, and start small with Asif's company's free counselling line.

qa.q: How might Asif feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Perhaps less judged, since Irawati shares a personal experience and offers a walk with no pressure.

grounding: A letter shows a young adult describing counselling as ordinary maintenance and explaining how to choose the right kind of help.

passage: Ishita, you asked, 'Aditi, why still see a therapist if you're fine now?' Okay. Two years ago I wasn't fine: panic on the metro, crying in office washrooms. Therapy helped a lot then. Now I go once a month, like servicing a scooter. Sometimes we talk about work, sometimes about my mother, sometimes about nothing much, and that's okay. I also found out therapy wasn't the only kind of help. When I was dealing with my father's drinking, a peer group for families of people with addiction helped in a way my therapist couldn't, because everyone there had lived it. I choose depending on what I need. And honestly, the monthly check-in catches things early. Last month I noticed I'd stopped cooking and was working till eleven. We caught it before it turned into a spiral. That's the whole point.

qa.q: How often does Aditi see the therapist now?
qa.a: Once a month.

qa.q: How does Aditi feel about therapy now compared with two years ago?
qa.a: Aditi sees it as calm, routine maintenance rather than crisis help, and seems at ease with it.

qa.q: How does Aditi choose the kind of help needed?
qa.a: By matching support to the need: regular therapy check-ins, and a peer group of families who had lived with addiction when that was the issue.

qa.q: Why might Ishita have been puzzled that Aditi still sees a therapist?
qa.a: Ishita may think therapy is only for when you are struggling, so it seemed odd when Aditi said things were fine.

grounding: A young adult explains to a friend how they use therapy as regular maintenance and choose peer support when it fits.

passage: I'm Pema, and I've shared a flat with Jyoti in Bengaluru for two years. Every second Thursday at six, she leaves for what she calls her "brain dentist". For a long time I assumed something was badly wrong. Once I asked, carefully, and she laughed. "Nothing's wrong. That's the point. I go so small things don't become big things." She had started after a hard breakup, she said, and kept going when life got better, the way you keep brushing after the toothache stops. I noticed she argued less with her mother on those Thursday nights, and she handled a bad appraisal in March without the week-long silence I'd seen before. She told me she had switched counsellors once, because the first one kept giving advice instead of listening. Last month, in my own rough patch, she didn't push. She just left her centre's number on the fridge. I called it on a Thursday.

qa.q: What does Jyoti call her counsellor?
qa.a: Her brain dentist.

qa.q: What might Jyoti have felt when Pema asked carefully about the Thursdays?
qa.a: Jyoti seemed relaxed and amused, laughing, not at all ashamed of going to therapy.

qa.q: What does Jyoti's approach show about choosing appropriate help?
qa.a: Treat counselling as regular maintenance, and switch counsellors if the fit is wrong, for example to one who listens rather than lectures.

qa.q: How has Pema's view of therapy changed?
qa.a: Pema first assumed something was badly wrong, but after seeing Jyoti handle hard moments calmly, Pema called the centre too.

grounding: A flatmate observes a young woman treating counselling as ordinary maintenance and choosing the right counsellor.

passage:
September. Rukmini had been snapping at everyone since her promotion. When Lalit suggested counselling, she laughed. "Therapy is for people with real problems." She tried to fix it with more gym.
October. Still sleeping badly, she went, half to prove Lalit wrong, to a free peer-support circle at the community centre. Eight people, one volunteer facilitator, no advice, just listening. A man her age described exactly the tight chest she felt every Sunday night. She didn't speak. But she came back the next week.
December. The facilitator mentioned that some things need more than a circle, and gave her the name of a counsellor with a sliding fee. Rukmini booked a first session, cancelled it, then booked again. By the end of the month she had been four times, and she still went to the circle on Tuesdays. She told Lalit, "It's like the gym, but for the part of me I kept ignoring."

qa.q: How many people were in the peer-support circle?
qa.a: Eight people.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when she booked, cancelled and rebooked the session?
qa.a: Rukmini felt hesitant and nervous about counselling, torn between old beliefs and needing help.

qa.q: How did the peer circle help Rukmini find the right level of help?
qa.a: It made her feelings seem normal, and its facilitator pointed her to a counsellor when more support was needed.

qa.q: How might Lalit feel hearing Rukmini's gym comparison?
qa.a: Lalit would likely feel relieved and quietly pleased that the suggestion she laughed at became something useful.

grounding: Over months, a young woman moves from dismissing therapy to peer support and then counselling as ordinary care.

passage: Harsha, you think I'm the calmest person in this office. Let your old colleague Maria tell you a secret. When I was twenty-five, my father died in the spring and I went back to work after four days, because that's what we did. I was fine, I told everyone. By autumn I was crying in the printer room and forgetting meetings. My friend Nalini said, "See someone." I said therapy was for weak people. She said, "Then call it maintenance, like servicing a scooter." I went, grumbling. The first counsellor was wrong for me: all questions about my childhood, nothing about now. I nearly quit. Nalini said, "Try another, the way you'd try another doctor." The second one helped. I went for two years, stopped, and went again when my son was born. So when you say you're "just stressed", Harsha, I'm only saying: servicing is not failure.

qa.q: How many days after her father's death did Maria go back to work?
qa.a: Four days.

qa.q: What was young Maria feeling by the autumn?
qa.a: Maria was overwhelmed and grieving, crying in the printer room and forgetting meetings.

qa.q: What choice in Maria's story made therapy work for her?
qa.a: Trying a second counsellor instead of quitting after a poor first fit, as she would with another doctor.

qa.q: How might Nalini have felt pushing Maria to see someone?
qa.a: Nalini was probably worried about her friend but patient, reframing therapy as maintenance to get past Maria's resistance.

grounding: A senior colleague tells a younger one how she came to see counselling as ordinary maintenance after grief.

passage:
For two months after the breakup, Vishal slept badly and snapped at everyone at work. He knew he needed someone to talk to. He also knew his savings were thin after paying for his sister's college admission.

At lunch, Ujjwal mentioned, as casually as if he were talking about the dentist, that he saw a counsellor every other Thursday. "Keeps the engine running," he said.

That evening Vishal searched and found two things: private therapists whose fees he couldn't manage right now, and a training clinic at the university's psychology department, where supervised counsellors charged according to income. There was a three-week wait.

He booked it anyway. He also joined a free weekly peer group run by a local volunteer centre, just to have somewhere to go in the meantime.

On the first Thursday, he sat in the waiting room with his knee jiggling. When the counsellor called his name, he stood up quickly, before he could change his mind.

qa.q: Where did Vishal find counselling he could afford?
qa.a: At a training clinic at the university's psychology department, where supervised counsellors charged according to income.

qa.q: How was Vishal feeling in the waiting room on the first Thursday?
qa.a: Vishal was nervous, with his knee jiggling, and a little afraid he might change his mind about going.

qa.q: What made Vishal's plan sensible given his thin savings?
qa.a: He chose a qualified, supervised clinic that charged according to income and used a free peer group while he waited, instead of giving up.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal's casual comment have affected Vishal?
qa.a: Hearing Ujjwal talk about counselling like a dentist visit likely made it feel ordinary and less embarrassing for Vishal to seek help.

grounding: A young man with little money treats counselling as ordinary care and finds affordable, appropriate help and a peer group.

passage:
The family lunch in Andheri was going well until Yash's phone buzzed with a reminder: Session, 5 p.m.

"Session of what?" his uncle asked.

"Therapy," Yash said, passing the raita. "Once a month."

His uncle put down his spoon. "Therapy? Is something wrong with you?"

"Nothing's wrong. I go to the gym for my back. I go to the counsellor for my head. It's maintenance."

A short silence. His aunt changed the subject to mangoes.

Later, on the balcony, his cousin Asif came out with two cups of tea. "Was that true? Just maintenance?"

"Mostly. When work gets bad, it helps to have someone who already knows the story."

Asif stared at the traffic. "My exams stuff is getting to me. How do I even find someone?"

"Check they're properly qualified, and meet one or two before you decide. If it doesn't feel right, try someone else. I'll send you where I started."

qa.q: How often does Yash go to therapy?
qa.a: Yash goes once a month.

qa.q: What might Asif have been feeling when he came out to the balcony?
qa.a: Asif was probably anxious and stressed about exams, and curious but a bit embarrassed to ask openly in front of the family.

qa.q: What advice did Yash give about choosing help, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Check that the counsellor is properly qualified and meet one or two before deciding, because the right fit matters for help to work.

qa.q: How does Yash's uncle see therapy at first?
qa.a: His uncle seems surprised and worried, assuming therapy means something is wrong, rather than seeing it as ordinary care.

grounding: A young man calmly describes therapy as routine maintenance at a family lunch and helps his cousin think about choosing appropriate help.

passage:
"I don't think I'm sick," Jyoti said, stirring her coffee. "I just cry on Sunday nights and I don't know anyone in this city."

Irfan nodded. "Okay. So what kind of help do you think you need?"

"That's the thing. Do I need a therapist? Or am I just lonely?"

"Maybe both. Maybe neither. What does your office offer?"

"There's a free counselling line. Six sessions."

"That's a good start. You can talk it through with someone trained, and they can tell you if you need more."

"And the loneliness?"

"There's that newcomers' group at the community centre on Saturdays. People who've just moved, like you. Peer support. Not therapy, but people."

Jyoti laughed shakily. "It feels weird. Like admitting I'm not coping."

"You'd see a doctor for a cough that won't go away. Same thing."

She took out her phone and opened the office website. "Six sessions. Fine. I'll call Monday."

qa.q: How many free counselling sessions does Jyoti's office offer?
qa.a: The free counselling line offers six sessions.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she said it was like admitting she was not coping?
qa.a: Jyoti felt embarrassed and uneasy about asking for help, as well as lonely and sad on Sunday nights.

qa.q: Which two kinds of help did Irfan suggest, and why do they fit?
qa.a: Irfan suggested the office counselling line for trained support and the newcomers' group for company, because Jyoti needs both someone trained and new people nearby.

qa.q: How might Irfan see Jyoti's worries?
qa.a: Irfan seems to see them as a normal reaction to moving to a new city, something to care for early rather than a sign of weakness.

grounding: Two young friends talk through the difference between counselling and peer support and choose ordinary, fitting help for loneliness.

passage:
The year I turned twenty-five, I got promoted and stopped sleeping. I told myself it was normal: new role, more pressure. My sister finally said, "You go to the dentist twice a year for your teeth. When did you last check on your head?"
I laughed, but it stuck. I found Nirmala through a clinic my company's insurance covered. She was a counsellor, not a psychiatrist; I'd checked the difference first, because I didn't think I needed medicine, just someone to talk to.
The first session I kept saying "I'm fine, just stressed." Nirmala asked, "What does stressed feel like in your body?" I didn't know. I'd never noticed.
We met every two weeks for six months. I learned to spot the tight jaw before the panic, and to say no to one extra project. Now I go once every couple of months, like servicing a scooter. I'm Kashish. It's not a crisis thing. It's maintenance.

qa.q: How often did Kashish meet Nirmala at first?
qa.a: Every two weeks for six months.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel in the first session?
qa.a: Kashish felt guarded and unsure, insisting on being fine and not knowing what stress felt like in the body.

qa.q: What did Kashish do well in choosing appropriate help?
qa.a: Kashish checked the difference between a counsellor and a psychiatrist and chose based on the need, using a clinic covered by insurance.

qa.q: How might Kashish's sister feel seeing therapy become routine?
qa.a: The sister probably feels relieved and glad the dentist comparison helped make it ordinary.

grounding: Shows a young adult treating counselling as ordinary maintenance and choosing the right kind of help.

passage:
Employee wellbeing note. Anand, HR wellbeing lead.
Divyansh, 24, came to ask about the company's counselling benefit, very quietly, as if asking about something illegal. He said his father had called therapy "for weak people".
I explained what we offer: six free sessions with a licensed counsellor, fully confidential; a peer-support circle on Thursdays run by trained colleagues; and, if needed, a referral to a psychiatrist through our insurance. I told him many people use it for ordinary things: stress, a breakup, a move.
He chose the peer circle first, to test the water. After three weeks, he booked counselling too.
Last week he told me he'd mentioned it to his father. "He didn't say much. But he asked if it helped." Divyansh looked lighter.
Plan: keep running the circle and share, anonymously, how many staff used the service this year, so it feels normal.

qa.q: How many free counselling sessions does the company offer?
qa.a: Six free sessions with a licensed counsellor.

qa.q: What does Divyansh asking very quietly suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Divyansh felt embarrassed and ashamed, as if seeking help were something to hide.

qa.q: Why was offering several types of help useful for Divyansh?
qa.a: It let him start with the least intimidating option, the peer circle, and move to counselling once he felt ready.

qa.q: How might Divyansh's father have felt asking if it helped?
qa.a: The father may have felt curious and less judgemental, perhaps quietly worried about his son.

grounding: Illustrates a workplace making counselling and peer support ordinary and a young adult choosing the help that fits.
